newsitem.title: USA: Controversy stalls U.S. Senate disaster aid bill.
newsitem.headline: Controversy stalls U.S. Senate disaster aid bill.

text.p: A Senate committee Tuesday postponed action on emergency spending for disaster victims when minority Democrats objected that Republicans were turning it into a vehicle for politically controversial issues.

Appropriations Committee Chairman Ted Stevens, R-Alaska, delayed action until Thursday after Democrat Robert Byrd of West Virginia objected to the bill. Stevens said the target for completion remains May 23, before the Memorial Day recess.

The bill would provide $5.5 billion for disaster relief and recovery in 20 states in the upper Midwest, Ohio Valley, Southeast and Pacific Northwest. Most of these states have experienced record-shattering floods.
In addition, it would provide $1.8 billion to pay for U.S. military operations in Bosnia and southwest Asia.

Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota told reporters Democratic objections centred on Republican-crafted proposals aimed at preventing future government shutdowns, which President Clinton has said he would veto.

"A couple of years ago -- you know, the Republicans shut the government down because they had a difference with the president. They're apparently willing to shut the disaster bill down for the same reason," Daschle said.

Called a permanent continuing resolution, the Republican provision would take the pressure off Congress to approve the 13 annual funding bills before the Oct. 1 start of the new fiscal year. No longer would government agencies face the prospect of running out of funds since their spending could continue indefinitely at the previous year's amount.

Stevens said Republican leaders wanted the anti-shutdown measure and a provision to stop the administration from using only union labour on construction contracts. Democrats also object to that provision.
A House committee has already approved an $8.4 billion emergency spending bill that will go to the House floor next week for a vote.
